newsitem.title: USA: Paraguay seeks release of U.S. death row inmate.
newsitem.headline: Paraguay seeks release of U.S. death row inmate.

text.p: Attorneys for Paraguay's government went to court in Virginia on Wednesday to contend that the U.S. state violated international law when it sentenced one of its citizens to death for rape and murder.

Paraguay is suing Virginia Gov. George Allen over the arrest of Angel Breard for the 1992 murder of a woman in Arlington and is asking the federal court to stop the execution and try Breard again with Paraguay's participation.

Donald Donovan, a lawyer representing Paraguay, told a three-judge panel of the Fourth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that Breard's rights under the Vienna Convention were violated because he was not told he had the right to contact Paraguayan authorities after his arrest.

Under Article 63 of the Vienna Convention, which the United States signed in 1963, aliens arrested in foreign countries must be told they have the right to contact the consul that represents their nation.
"So long as he remains in prison, so long as he faces execution, there is continuing harm to Paraguay ... and we're entitled to relief," Donovan said.

Senior Assistant Attorney General Donald Curry called the inmate's contention an attempt to circumvent legal procedure because he never raised the claim in state court. He also warned that if Breard prevailed on appeal, there was a danger he might walk away a free man because he could not be tried again for the same crime.
"We're not dealing with a burglar here. We're dealing with an admitted capital murderer," Curry said.
Breard was convicted in 1993 for the February 16, 1992, rape and murder of Ruth Dickie, of Arlington, Virginia.
There are at least 30 other foreign inmates on U.S. death rows who allege their treaty rights were not honoured after their arrests, according to lawyers.

None of the foreign nationals who have made the claim have won a new trial, but attorneys have said the Richmond case is different because it is a foreign government, not a death row defendant, alleging that its treaty rights were violated.
Richmond U.S. District Court Judge Richard Williams ruled against Paraguay last November, although he said he was troubled by Virginia's failure to follow international law.
He ruled he had no authority to hear the case because the 11th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution bars suits in federal court by foreign governments against American states.
